The trigger parser could be materially sharper if it also parsed an *event/date gate* from the trigger text (e.g. "after 7/22-23") and suppressed or down-weighted the alert until that date passes, rather than firing on the price alone. That would save event-driven runs for triggers whose *conditions*, not just prices, are met — reducing exactly this kind of "premature trigger" cycle.

** The single highest-value fix this run is upstream of my judgment: the orchestrator handed me a portfolio reading `$0 equity / $0 cash / no positions` with no `data_quality` or `stale_data_notice` flag raised, even though the trade history mathematically implies ~$9,820 should exist. A cheap deterministic guard — "if broker equity is ~$0 but closed-trade math implies non-trivial cash, flag `broker_sync_suspect` and set `allows_new_buys: false` with a reason" — would prevent a future run from being invited to trade (this was even a trigger-driven run) against an account it cannot possibly fund, and would save me from spending the cycle diagnosing broker plumbing instead of setups. Separately, the watchlist trigger checker should parse the *qualitative* half of `would_buy_at` (here, "confirmed positive reaction to the 7/22-23 event... not a bounce off today's low") rather than only the first dollar figure, so it stops firing event-driven runs on price alone before the event has occurred.

** Two concrete data defects cost me real research time and nearly cost me a bad trade.

`gap_analysis` reports a gap's size, direction, and whether it later filled, but not how the session actually closed relative to its open — so UNH shows an unfilled +7.4% gap while `pct_change_1d` is only +1.16%, meaning most of the pop was sold intraday, and I had to infer that from two fields that don't reconcile on their face. A `close_vs_open_pct` (or an `intraday_fade` flag) on the gap object would let an evening review distinguish a *held* gap from a *faded* one, which is the entire difference between a real drift setup and a failed print — precisely the call I had to hedge on UNH tonight. Weekly self-review: This week was mostly build week, not trade week - the system went from a bare skeleton to a full pipeline (data relay, validator, position sizing, watchlist triggers, insider activity, sector relative strength, post-earnings drift detection) in a handful of commits, and only opened its first two live paper positions on 7/9 (DELL) and 7/10 (HPE). Neither has closed yet, so there is no win/loss to grade - the real test of the process comes next week when these mature past a few days and I have to apply the cash-test and thesis-break discipline for real, not just in theory. What I got right: discipline held under pressure - six separate runs today all correctly said no-trade rather than forcing a mediocre setup into a rate-driven, breadth-thin tape, and both live entries were valuation-anchored (12-20x forward earnings) rather than chases into the 40-170x names topping the momentum scan. What went wrong was mostly data quality, not reasoning: the insider Form-4 feed got flagged as noisy five separate times this week because financial-sponsor distributions (Silver Lake's Dell unwind, ALAB's post-lockup sales) bury genuine officer-conviction signals under hundreds of routine rows, a stale next_earnings field showed a past date for HPE, and the post_earnings_drift_candidate flag missed HPE's textbook drift setup because a one-time GAAP charge masked rising estimates - all bad data, not bad judgment, but they cost research time I'd rather spend on names. The one change for next week: get the insider feed pre-classified into sponsor/10b5-1 vs. discretionary officer transactions before it's handed to me, since that single fix has been the most repeated friction point of the week and is pure engineering, not agent judgment.

** The insider_activity feed is dominated by financial-sponsor unwinds (Silver Lake's programmatic Dell distribution ran to 79 separate line items) and routine 10b5-1 officer sales, which bury any genuinely informative *open-market* signal. A pre-computed classifier flag distinguishing "sponsor/PE distribution" and "scheduled 10b5-1" from "discretionary open-market officer buy/sell," plus a net cluster-buy score, would let me weight this data in seconds instead of scrolling hundreds of near-identical sell tickets to conclude "no signal."

** The insider_activity feed lumps financial-sponsor distributions (Silver Lake's DELL unwind, ALAB's pre-arranged director sales) in with genuine operating-insider signals, forcing me to manually parse dozens of near-identical rows to conclude "not a real signal." A pre-computed classification — tagging each cluster as sponsor/10b5-1-scheduled vs. discretionary officer transaction, and netting to a single per-ticker signal — would make the "clustered officer buying vs. routine selling" judgment the rules ask for far faster and less error-prone.

** The `post_earnings_drift_candidate` flag was `false` for HPE even though it fits the textbook drift profile the bundle prioritizes (record quarter just reported, +40% EPS revisions, price still 24% below its high). The detector appears to have been distorted by HPE's GAAP net *loss* last quarter — a one-time Juniper acquisition charge — which masked the underlying estimate momentum. Adding a "GAAP charge / acquisition-adjusted" screen (or keying the drift flag off EPS-revision magnitude and days-since-earnings rather than reported net income sign) would have surfaced this run's best idea automatically instead of leaving me to reconstruct it by hand.

** The context bundle's per-candidate `next_earnings` field is unreliable — HPE's showed `2026-06-01` (already past) while the `days_to_earnings`/`days_since_earnings` fields correctly implied the next print is in September. These two sources disagreeing forced me to reason around it; the run would be cleaner if `next_earnings` were validated to always be a *future* date (or dropped in favor of the days-based fields), so the earnings-clock gate can't be tripped by a stale value.

** The `insider_activity` feed is dominated by non-signal noise — Silver Lake's sponsor-distribution selling in DELL and Alba/Dyckerhoff post-lockup selling in ALAB swamp the data with hundreds of routine rows, which buries any genuinely informative *officer* buying/selling. This run would have been sharper if the context bundle pre-classified Form 4s (e.g., tagging financial-sponsor/10%-owner distributions and post-IPO-lockup sales separately from discretionary open-market C-suite transactions) and surfaced a net "discretionary officer" buy/sell tally per ticker, so clustered insider *conviction* signals aren't drowned out by mechanical unwinds.
